title: Two Clocks in Diffusion MLLMs:When Answers Stabilize Before Rationales Unfold

paper.title: Two Clocks in Diffusion MLLMs: When Answers Stabilize Before Rationales Unfold
paper.abstract: Abstract An answer candidate in a masked diffusion MLLM can stabilize while its rationale is still unfolding. We distinguish retrospective stabilization of the logged candidate from token commitment, and examine these two clocks relative to rationale generation. Analyzing our results across three visual question-answering benchmarks, we find that 89.4–98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs. On V*Bench, reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%, together with answer coverage and the eligible observation window. Under EOS-enabled prompting, direct instructions improve Nemotron’s overall accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M 3 CoT and ScienceQA, but reduce LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points. A symmetric decomposition associates the larger absolute component of each change with coverage rather than conditional accuracy. Matched-canvas image ablations measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization, separating the two temporal readouts. Together, these measurements distinguish answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity, and identify coverage as the larger component of the prompting differences.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A rationale printed before an answer appears to document the steps that produced it. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting can improve task performance [ 1 ] , but the order and content of an explanation need not faithfully reveal the computation behind an answer [ 2 , 3 ] . In masked diffusion generation, this distinction is especially concrete: a token displayed late in the final response may be predicted, or even permanently written, before tokens displayed earlier. Iterative masked decoding exposes a useful observation point. At a still-masked answer position, the decoder has a candidate token even when its scheduler does not yet select that position for commitment [ 4 , 5 ] . We distinguish two events: T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} , when the logged candidate first matches the final answer and never subsequently departs from it on observable steps, and T commit T_{\mathrm{commit}} , when that answer position becomes permanent. Stabilization is computed retrospectively from the recorded trajectory. Early answer convergence and answer-first commitment are already documented [ 5 , 6 , 8 ] . We examine when answers stabilize relative to the unfolding rationale, alongside visual sensitivity and valid-answer coverage. Here, unfolding refers to the commitment of rationale-side tokens to the canvas. Figure 1 separates the two answer clocks from the visual-sensitivity diagnostic. Figure 1: Overview of the measurement protocol. (a) Hold the model and input fixed, vary the block schedule, and record the decoding trace. (b) Distinguish stabilization of the logged answer candidate, T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} , from permanent token commitment, T commit T_{\mathrm{commit}} ; the image-ablation peak T PDM T_{\mathrm{PDM}} is a separate diagnostic. (c-i) Measure the unwritten fraction U U of the rationale-side region ℛ \mathcal{R} at T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} . (c-ii) Compare image-present and image-removed token distributions on the same pre-step canvas and mask pattern. The PDM readout region is defined in Section 3.3 . The trace and curve are schematic illustrations. After commitment, a logged candidate may be copied from the canvas. Here PDM t = D t \mathrm{PDM}_{t}=D_{t} in Equation 3 . A short-block schedule can make the answer position observable only after earlier text is written. A decreasing image-ablation signal can reflect information already in the canvas. An accuracy gain can arise chiefly because more responses contain extractable answers. None of these distinctions is visible in the completed rationale alone. Our analysis connects three observations. First, the LaViDa block control links a fall in the unwritten fraction from 89.4% to 1.7% to changed answer-slot eligibility and lower answer coverage. Second, matched-canvas image ablations give configuration-dependent peak locations that cannot be substituted for answer stabilization. Third, coverage contributes the larger absolute term in all five prompting comparisons, including the LaViDa accuracy loss. Building on earlier convergence and commitment-order studies, these results characterize how rationale generation relates to answer stability, visual sensitivity, and answer availability under the evaluated decoding policies.

sections.heading: Early convergence and commitment order.
sections.text: Li et al. [5] study early answer convergence and introduce Prophet, an early-commit decoder. Their main convergence analysis tracks the first ground-truth-token match on finally correct outputs; their appendix also examines changes on incorrect outputs. Our target is a stable suffix matching the output’s own final token on eligible logged steps. We use this distinction between prediction and commitment to examine how multimodal rationales unfold under explicit scheduling and stopping conditions. Yeom et al. [6] study answer-first commitment, finite-canvas backfill, and positional restrictions. They also delay a reserved answer position and compare against a timing-matched reasoning-token delay. Our additional focus is the relationship to image-ablation sensitivity and to valid-answer coverage.

sections.heading: Visual grounding and rationale faithfulness.
sections.text: Favero et al. [7] introduce visual Prompt Dependency Measure (PDM), including its Hellinger-distance form PDM-H, for autoregressive VLMs. Thinking Diffusion [ 8 ] applies visual PDM to diffusion MLLMs, reports early answer generation and weak early visual dependence, and proposes Position and Step Penalty (PSP) and Visual Reasoning Guidance (VRG). We use matched-canvas distribution comparisons to measure the relationship between visual-sensitivity peaks and answer stabilization. ST-Veto [ 9 ] uses second-order Taylor residuals of token confidence and image-attention mass to veto and replace unmasking candidates. Its online confidence-stability criterion differs from our retrospective final-token stability, and its attention-based grounding signal differs from our image-ablation distribution comparison. Turpin et al. [ 2 ] show that explanations can omit input biases that influence answers; Lanham et al. [ 3 ] intervene on CoT content to measure answer dependence.

sections.heading: Multimodal diffusion systems.
sections.text: LaViDa [ 10 ] , the Nemotron diffusion vision-language path [ 11 ] , and DiffusionGemma [ 12 ] provide different decoding implementations. We analyze answer timing in LaViDa, prompting and visual sensitivity in LaViDa and Nemotron, and an additional prompting comparison in DiffusionGemma.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental setup
sections.text: We analyze V*Bench (191 examples), a fine-grained visual-search benchmark [ 13 ] ; M 3 CoT (400 examples), a multimodal multi-step benchmark [ 14 ] ; and an image-containing ScienceQA subset (400 examples) [ 15 ] . Appendix B.1 gives the instruction templates. The primary LaViDa timing condition uses a 128-token canvas, 64 denoising steps, one block, greedy candidate selection, and EOS suppression. Its V*Bench control changes block length to 8. The Nemotron timing comparisons disable the confidence early-exit shortcut and suppress EOS. Approximate dLLM-Cache is disabled in the traced settings, while fixed-prefix caches can still be used. Suppressing EOS permits full-canvas timing analysis. Prompting results allow EOS and compare matched configured budgets within each model, using a shared scorer. For Nemotron and DiffusionGemma, the reasoning-requested prefix asks for <think> -tagged reasoning followed by an answer; the direct prefix requests only an option letter. Thus explanation instructions and response-format constraints change together. The LaViDa and Nemotron comparisons use 128 tokens/64 steps; DiffusionGemma retains its own sampler. Timing localization maps the answer letter to its containing token. Output scoring separately strips echoed prompts, prioritizes explicit declarations, and uses a case-sensitive bare-letter fallback. We analyze aggregate experimental results using the measurement definitions in Section 3 . Timing means are conditional on valid localization; coverage and overall accuracy use the full evaluated set. We conducted the experiments on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Appendices A – C specify the extraction and aggregation rules, prompt templates, dataset interfaces, and decoding controls. We compare the results across these decoding configurations; Section 5.2 presents our correctness-stratified statistical tests.

sections.heading: Answer stability and rationale unfolding.
sections.text: The two clocks separate candidate stabilization from permanent token commitment. In single-block LaViDa decoding, the mean stabilization time precedes the mean commitment time on all three benchmarks, while 89.4–98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization. The answer candidate is stable during a substantial portion of subsequent rationale generation. The relationship between the clock gap and rationale progress is particularly clear when comparing M 3 CoT and ScienceQA. The difference of clock means is smaller on M 3 CoT (6.67 versus 10.22 steps), yet its unwritten fraction is larger (98.1% versus 96.2%). The clock gap measures separation between two events at the answer position, whereas U U summarizes commitment across the rationale-side positions at stabilization. These readouts capture different aspects of the same trajectory. Equation 2 connects them through the rationale-side commitment distribution: evaluating its cumulative fraction at T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} gives the written fraction, and taking the complement gives U U . This relationship explains the role of U U alongside the two clocks in the timing tables.

sections.heading: Scheduling and visual sensitivity.
sections.text: The short-block control shifts both answer clocks later and reduces the unwritten fraction to 1.7%. The PDM comparisons measure a separate temporal property: the step at which image removal changes token distributions most strongly. On Nemotron, mean PDM peak times follow mean answer stabilization times on all three benchmarks. On LaViDa, the mean PDM peak precedes mean stabilization on V*Bench and ScienceQA, while the two means are close on M 3 CoT. PDM compares full vocabulary distributions, whereas stabilization follows one token identity. Changes in distributional sensitivity and persistence of the answer candidate are therefore compatible.

sections.heading: Coverage and prompting.
sections.text: Direct prompting raises Nemotron and DiffusionGemma accuracy and lowers LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy. In each comparison, the coverage-associated term is the larger absolute component of the accuracy change. Reporting C C , Q Q , and A A together makes this pattern explicit: the prompting differences involve both accepted-answer frequency and correctness among accepted answers.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: The block control exposes a trade-off between generation order and task performance. Reducing the block length lowers U U from 89.4% to 1.7%, while coverage falls from 100.0% to 91.6% and overall accuracy from 41.9% to 39.8%. More positional commitment therefore accompanies lower answer coverage and accuracy in this comparison. Direct prompting also has opposing effects across models: the accuracy gains on Nemotron and DiffusionGemma contrast with the 11.0-point loss on LaViDa/V*Bench.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: In single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa decoding, answers stabilize before most rationale-side tokens are committed. Short blocks move both answer clocks later and sharply reduce the unwritten fraction. Image-ablation peaks occupy distinct mean step locations from answer stabilization. Direct prompting improves Nemotron and DiffusionGemma accuracy but reduces LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy, with coverage providing the larger arithmetic component in all five comparisons. Reading a rationale together with its commitment trace reveals two orderings: the order in which the explanation is presented and the order in which the model makes its output tokens permanent. The two clocks distinguish answer stability from commitment and connect both to the unfolding of the rationale.

Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Hanyang University, Seoul, Korea Email: {ktkpv94,cys}@hanyang.ac.kr Abstract An answer candidate in a masked diffusion MLLM can stabilize while its rationale is still unfolding. We distinguish retrospective stabilization of the logged candidate from token commitment, and examine these two clocks relative to rationale generation. Analyzing our results across three visual question-answering benchmarks, we find that 89.4–98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs. On V*Bench, reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%, together with answer coverage and the eligible observation window. Under EOS-enabled prompting, direct instructions improve Nemotron’s overall accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M 3 CoT and ScienceQA, but reduce LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points. A symmetric decomposition associates the larger absolute component of each change with coverage rather than conditional accuracy. Matched-canvas image ablations measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization, separating the two temporal readouts. Together, these measurements distinguish answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity, and identify coverage as the larger component of the prompting differences. 1 Introduction A rationale printed before an answer appears to document the steps that produced it. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting can improve task performance [ 1 ] , but the order and content of an explanation need not faithfully reveal the computation behind an answer [ 2 , 3 ] . In masked diffusion generation, this distinction is especially concrete: a token displayed late in the final response may be predicted, or even permanently written, before tokens displayed earlier. Iterative masked decoding exposes a useful observation point. At a still-masked answer position, the decoder has a candidate token even when its scheduler does not yet select that position for commitment [ 4 , 5 ] . We distinguish two events: T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} , when the logged candidate first matches the final answer and never subsequently departs from it on observable steps, and T commit T_{\mathrm{commit}} , when that answer position becomes permanent. Stabilization is computed retrospectively from the recorded trajectory. Early answer convergence and answer-first commitment are already documented [ 5 , 6 , 8 ] . We examine when answers stabilize relative to the unfolding rationale, alongside visual sensitivity and valid-answer coverage. Here, unfolding refers to the commitment of rationale-side tokens to the canvas. Figure 1 separates the two answer clocks from the visual-sensitivity diagnostic. Figure 1: Overview of the measurement protocol. (a) Hold the model and input fixed, vary the block schedule, and record the decoding trace. (b) Distinguish stabilization of the logged answer candidate, T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} , from permanent token commitment, T commit T_{\mathrm{commit}} ; the image-ablation peak T PDM T_{\mathrm{PDM}} is a separate diagnostic. (c-i) Measure the unwritten fraction U U of the rationale-side region ℛ \mathcal{R} at T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} . (c-ii) Compare image-present and image-removed token distributions on the same pre-step canvas and mask pattern. The PDM readout region is defined in Section 3.3 . The trace and curve are schematic illustrations. After commitment, a logged candidate may be copied from the canvas. Here PDM t = D t \mathrm{PDM}_{t}=D_{t} in Equation 3 . A short-block schedule can make the answer position observable only after earlier text is written. A decreasing image-ablation signal can reflect information already in the canvas. An accuracy gain can arise chiefly because more responses contain extractable answers. None of these distinctions is visible in the completed rationale alone. Our analysis connects three observations. First, the LaViDa block control links a fall in the unwritten fraction from 89.4% to 1.7% to changed answer-slot eligibility and lower answer coverage. The two clocks separate candidate stabilization from permanent token commitment. In single-block LaViDa decoding, the mean stabilization time precedes the mean commitment time on all three benchmarks, while 89.4–98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization. The answer candidate is stable during a substantial portion of subsequent rationale generation. The relationship between the clock gap and rationale progress is particularly clear when comparing M 3 CoT and ScienceQA. The difference of clock means is smaller on M 3 CoT (6.67 versus 10.22 steps), yet its unwritten fraction is larger (98.1% versus 96.2%). The clock gap measures separation between two events at the answer position, whereas U U summarizes commitment across the rationale-side positions at stabilization. These readouts capture different aspects of the same trajectory. Equation 2 connects them through the rationale-side commitment distribution: evaluating its cumulative fraction at T stab T_{\mathrm{stab}} gives the written fraction, and taking the complement gives U U . This relationship explains the role of U U alongside the two clocks in the timing tables. Scheduling and visual sensitivity. The short-block control shifts both answer clocks later and reduces the unwritten fraction to 1.7%. The PDM comparisons measure a separate temporal property: the step at which image removal changes token distributions most strongly. On Nemotron, mean PDM peak times follow mean answer stabilization times on all three benchmarks. On LaViDa, the mean PDM peak precedes mean stabilization on V*Bench and ScienceQA, while the two means are close on M 3 CoT. PDM compares full vocabulary distributions, whereas stabilization follows one token identity. Changes in distributional sensitivity and persistence of the answer candidate are therefore compatible. Coverage and prompting. Direct prompting raises Nemotron and DiffusionGemma accuracy and lowers LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy. In each comparison, the coverage-associated term is the larger absolute component of the accuracy change. Reporting C C , Q Q , and A A together makes this pattern explicit: the prompting differences involve both accepted-answer frequency and correctness among accepted answers. 7 Limitations The block control exposes a trade-off between generation order and task performance. Reducing the block length lowers U U from 89.4% to 1.7%, while coverage falls from 100.0% to 91.6% and overall accuracy from 41.9% to 39.8%. More positional commitment therefore accompanies lower answer coverage and accuracy in this comparison. Direct prompting also has opposing effects across models: the accuracy gains on Nemotron and DiffusionGemma contrast with the 11.0-point loss on LaViDa/V*Bench. 8 Conclusion In single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa decoding, answers stabilize before most rationale-side tokens are committed. Short blocks move both answer clocks later and sharply reduce the unwritten fraction. Image-ablation peaks occupy distinct mean step locations from answer stabilization. Direct prompting improves Nemotron and DiffusionGemma accuracy but reduces LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy, with coverage providing the larger arithmetic component in all five comparisons. Reading a rationale together with its commitment trace reveals two orderings: the order in which the explanation is presented and the order in which the model makes its output tokens permanent. The two clocks distinguish answer stability from commitment and connect both to the unfolding of the rationale.
